subject: Anatomy
summary: The vermiform appendix is a narrow, blind-ended tube attached to the cecum. Its position varies, influencing clinical signs in inflammation. Though its function is limited, it can harbor disease that mimics many abdominal conditions.

sections.p: A 5–10 cm tubular structure arising from the posteromedial cecum, just below the ileocecal valve. It is covered by peritoneum and contains lymphoid tissue.
The base is 2–3 cm from the ileocecal valve; the tip may be retrocecal, pelvic, subhepatic, or pre‑ileal. Wall layers mirror the rest of the colon but are thinner.
b: Mucosa: simple columnar epithelium with goblet cells

sections.p: Depending on tip position, the appendix contacts the iliopsoas muscle, obturator internus, uterus, fallopian tubes, or the right ovary, explaining specific clinical signs.
Arises from the appendicular artery, a branch of the ileocolic artery (superior mesenteric). Venous drainage follows the same route to the portal system.
b: Vein: drains into superior mesenteric vein

sections.p: Visceral afferents travel with the superior mesenteric plexus; somatic pain from the serosa is conveyed by the lower thoracic (T10‑T12) intercostal nerves.
b: Somatic pain: localized right lower quadrant

sections.p: Acts as a reservoir for gut flora and contributes to mucosal immunity via its lymphoid tissue, especially in early life.
Appendicitis is the most common surgical emergency. Position determines signs (psoas, obturator) and risk of perforation. Other pathologies include carcinoid tumor, mucocele, and parasitic infection.
b: Acute appendicitis: inflammation starts in mucosa, may spread to serosa
Appendiceal carcinoid: <2 cm usually cured by appendectomy

t.b: Does the appendix appear non‑compressible >6 mm? Positive suggests appendicitis; a normal appendix does not rule it out.
Shows enlarged appendix, peri‑appendiceal fat stranding, or perforation. If unavailable, rely on clinical signs and plain X‑ray for free air.
Elevated >12 ×10⁹/L supports infection but can be normal in early disease or immunocompromised patients.

sections.p: Key points to remember for exams and bedside assessment.
b: McBurney’s point tenderness = base of appendix

whenToSeekHelp: Severe right lower quadrant pain with fever
Vomiting, inability to pass gas, or shock

faq.q: Why does appendicitis start as vague periumbilical pain?
faq.a: Visceral afferents from the appendix travel with T10, which supplies the umbilical region.

faq.q: Can the appendix be removed prophylactically?
faq.a: Elective removal is not recommended unless there is a tumor, mucocele, or chronic inflammation.

faq.q: What is the significance of a yellow tip lesion on the appendix?
faq.a: A bright yellow lesion often represents a fecalith, a common obstructing cause of acute appendicitis.

exam: Describe how the position of the appendix influences physical‑exam findings.
List the stepwise diagnostic approach to suspected acute appendicitis in a low‑resource setting.
